Implementing Post-Quantum Secure
Exotic Signature Schemes in Blockchains

LAS — a lattice adaptor signature built on CRYSTALS-Dilithium primitives: implemented twice, benchmarked against two baselines, and demonstrated end-to-end in a post-quantum atomic swap.

Royce StevenSupervisor: Dr Zhipeng Wangevidence run 20260804_101750
The problem

Post-quantum blockchains have the basic signatures.
They do not have the exotic ones.

Today

Every chain signs with ECDSA, Schnorr or BLS — all elliptic-curve.

Shor breaks all three.

Standardised

NIST has ML-DSA and friends — basic signatures.

A basic signature authenticates a message and nothing more.

Missing

Multi-sig, threshold, adaptor — the schemes that give chains their features.

Post-quantum: mostly paper-only, no working code.

This project turns one paper design — LAS, a lattice adaptor signature — into a tested, benchmarked, blockchain-facing artefact.

The mechanism · four functions added to a plain signature

Publishing a signature leaks a secret — that is what makes a swap atomic

STEP 1
PreSign
σ̂ = (c, ẑ)
Verifies against a statement Y — but is not a spendable signature.
STEP 2
Adapt
z = ẑ + y
Whoever knows the witness y completes it into an ordinary signature.
STEP 3
Publish
σ → chain
On chain it is an ordinary payment. No script, no hash lock, nothing to see.
STEP 4
Extract
y = z − ẑ
The counterparty subtracts and recovers y — which unlocks the other leg.

Two chains, no trusted third party, no on-chain script: both legs settle or neither does.

Why the numbers are trustworthy

Rejection attempts are counted, never inferred from timing: 2.615 per Sign against 2.724 per PreSign.

Every run aborts unless that matches the closed-form model within five standard errors — and correctness is asserted on the very objects about to be timed.

Scope: mean ± SD over 5 repetitions × 500/1000 iterations, C implementation, one machine. At the packed byte boundary the premium rises to +20.7–90.0% — that is serialization, not adaptor arithmetic.

Inside a LAS signature (6736 B at the target set)

response z — 99.3% challenge digest c̃ — 0.7%

The challenge travels only as its digest, so optimising LAS means optimising z.

And an adaptor swap adds one public object

The statement Y — 4416 B, exactly the size of a public key — plus a signature-sized pre-signature.

Those are the only objects an adaptor scheme sends that a basic signature does not.

Fairness: the classical baseline is a functionality-matched ECDSA adaptor signature (not plain ECDSA), compared at Simplified Dilithium-II — an engineering match to ≈128-bit, not a formal security-equivalence claim.

The controlled comparison

Same signature, same relation, same pinned inputs — only the prover changes.

Swapping Groth16 for the lattice prover: 53.1% faster, 61.9% larger.

Strip the proof out

The entire post-quantum signature workload of a swap — two key generations, two pre-signatures, two adaptations, an extraction, two settlements — is about 5.5× the classical one.

A factor of five on a millisecond workload is unremarkable.

Communication, again

A fully post-quantum swap moves about 85.1× the bytes and puts 63.1× more on the ledgers.

On a UTXO chain that is the multiple that costs money.

Demonstration 2 of 2 · a real Bitcoin Core v31.1 node, on regtest

It fits the size limits. It fails the verification rules — so I changed one.

▶ SCREEN CAPTURE — the node's own output
BTC_TAG · BTC_SRC · BTC_BIN_PATCHED · BTC_BIN_STOCK
then scripts/run_btc_las_node.sh — full line in VIDEO_PLAN
Show: the patched node rejecting a mutated spend while a stock node accepts it — side by side. That differential is the whole argument.

1 · Carriage, stock node

A lattice-carrying spend: 2,939 vB, refused by default relay policy (bad-witness-nonstandard) — yet consensus-valid, and mined.

Standardness and validity are different questions; only the second decides feasibility.

2 · Verification, patched node

Opcode 0xbb defined as lattice verification: a spend with no elliptic-curve signature at all was accepted and mined (2,917 vB).

9 mutations refused by the patched node and accepted by a stock one — which attributes the refusals to the new rule.

Honest limits: a patched node is not Bitcoin, so “cannot settle on Bitcoin as it stands” still holds; the security of the new rule is not analysed; and it is not wired into the swap.

The negative result that turned over · EVM, real client receipt

“Impossible on chain” was an inference, not a measurement

What I measured first

A complete, validated native verifier: ≈56.6 M gas — over the EIP-7825 cap. The optimistic variant then moved the cost into a fraud proof that also exceeds it.

What I got wrong

I recorded the cause as structural and inferred that local optimisation could not close the gap. Re-expressing the same predicate closed it.

A real client mined a claim running full verification at 16,413,275 gas — 97.8% of the cap.

Scope is part of the claim: Simplified Dilithium-III, a 32-byte signed message, that EVM revision. The remaining margin is a message-length budget, and no other parameter set was evaluated.

Testing a design decision instead of asserting it · LAS on unmodified FIPS 204

The belief the whole implementation rested on was half wrong

Naive port fails

0/200
pre-signatures verify when the statement is only added to the hash

So some modification is genuinely unavoidable.

But the verifier need not change

200/200
accepted by the unmodified FIPS 204 verifier once the whole commitment path moves onto w + Y

PreSign and PreVerify are new algorithms. Verify is not.

It relocates the bottleneck

Signature falls 6736 → 3309 B, but the statement Y is byte-identical (4416 B).

Compressing the signature makes Y the dominant object rather than removing it.

Functional demonstration only: whether committing to HighBits(w + Y) preserves ML-DSA's unforgeability is not analysed — that is the prerequisite before this route could be recommended.

Negative results · measured, not speculated

Three optimisations, implemented and closed — each names the mechanism that beat it

Compress the statement Y

Truncation is invisible to the adaptor's own functions — they hash whatever statement they are handed — and fatal at ordinary Verify and at Extract, which accepts only on the exact relation.

Deriving Y from a seed compresses it totally and hands over the witness.

Amortise the proof over a batch

Groth16's proof is constant in batch size — so bytes were never the bottleneck to amortise.

The lattice prover's per-swap proof shrinks, but proving and verifying get several times worse.

Optimistic on-chain verification

The honest claim becomes cheap (≈1.2 M gas), but the worst-case fraud proof costs ≈28.2 M — over the cap.

A fraud proof that cannot be mined is not a fraud proof.

An untested future-work bullet costs nothing to write and tells a reader nothing. These close two of the three directions outright.

Conclusion

A post-quantum adaptor signature is achievable by reuse.
The bill arrives in bytes.

What the evidence supports

  • All five objectives met; the lattice core reused unchanged, validated by a second independent implementation.
  • Adaptor functionality: at most +8.3% of computation at the core boundary.
  • The real cost is communication — z and the statement Y.
  • In a real swap the proof consumes over 98% of the work.

What stays open

  • A hard relation whose statement is small by design — not a better encoding.
  • A proof system succinct at this scale, not only asymptotically.
  • The security of the ML-DSA variant, and of the consensus rule.
  • A live network: for the post-quantum legs the blocker is a consensus rule, not engineering.

No concrete security is formally analysed and nothing settled on a live network — both scoped out by design, and both bound what these numbers mean.
